title: Breaking the top off a hill: what is behind the hole
question: Does the opened ground now read as sky, and is the shading on its right-hand side — where the taller slope stands over it — right, too strong, or too weak?
context_md:
Your report: *"the background remains black ... looks bad when I break up the ground near the surface"*.

**What was wrong.** The darkness behind a void was a function of **how far the light had travelled** from the last place that was open. Distance cannot tell a hole from a hollow, so a wide cut with most of the sky still overhead scored the same as a slot you can barely stand in — the design round's own table has them at 0.023 and 0.010.

**What it does now.** Each place also asks *how much of the sky can I actually see*, along eight directions, dimmed only by rock it has to pass through. A mine still goes dark at any width, because a slot admits a sliver of sky and nothing more.

**The left tile of each pane is the hill before it was cut** — the same shot, for reference. Zoom out (`z`) to see both.

**What I am unsure about** is the second half of the question. The dimming down the right of the cut is the taller ground beside it genuinely blocking that side of the sky. I do not know whether it reads as shade or as smog. Ignore the plants and the water line; nothing here touched either.
